text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are computer programs trained to understand and generate human language. They work by analyzing text word by word, using patterns learned from enormous amounts of data—books, websites, and articles—to predict the next most likely word in a sequence. Training involves feeding the model billions of examples so it can recognize grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns. To use an LLM effectively, you practice prompt engineering: writing clear, specific instructions or questions to get better responses. These models are impressive—they can write essays, summarize texts, translate languages, and even code. However, they have limits. They can invent facts (called hallucinations), lack true understanding, and may reflect biases from their training data. So, while powerful, they are tools, not flawless thinkers.
